title: Faithfulness in marriage
hook: fidelity in marriage as part of rehat

segments.voice: Yesterday, why no intoxicants: one wine refused, and another, the Name, offered. Your line was clear mind. When did you pause before reaching for something? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-three.

A ring on a kitchen windowsill, set down while someone does the dishes. A kara on a wrist, never taken off at all. Two small circles, two kinds of promise. We've spent this stretch of the path on the Sikh code, and most of it has looked outward: what to wear, what to eat, what to drink, how to bow. Today's rule lives somewhere quieter. It isn't visible on a street or in a gurdwara hall. It lives at home, between two people, on ordinary days when nobody else is watching. The code names faithfulness in marriage as part of a Sikh's rehat, a Sikh's way of living. So today: why does a code about turbans and prayers also reach into a marriage?
screen: `A RING ON A WINDOWSILL.` → `A KARA ON A WRIST.` → `A RULE THAT LIVES AT HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. The Rehat Maryada asks a Sikh to keep to their own spouse, and to look on other people with respect: in paraphrase, a man is to regard another's wife as his mother or sister, and a woman another's husband as her father or brother. Adultery is named among the four things the initiated must never do. It sits on the same short list as cutting the hair and using tobacco. That placement says something. For a Sikh who has taken amrit, faithfulness is as much a part of the vow as the kesh. Second, the picture behind it. In a verse by Guru Amar Das on Ang 788, in paraphrase: they are not called husband and wife who merely sit together. They are husband and wife who are one light in two bodies. That's the whole idea in one line. A marriage isn't two people sharing a house. It's one light living in two forms. Third, the portrait of a good life in the Sukhmani Sahib, on Ang 274, includes eyes that do not dwell on another's spouse. Faithfulness there starts small: with where the eyes rest, long before anything happens. And fourth, notice how it fits the Anand Karaj, the wedding we met earlier in this block. The couple walk around the Guru Granth Sahib together, and the hymns of that walk are about the soul's marriage to God. Some readers hear the two marriages leaning on each other: keeping faith with a spouse as practice for keeping faith with God, and the other way around. On that reading, the vow at home and the vow to the Guru are the same kind of promise.
screen: `ADULTERY: ONE OF THE FOUR AVOIDED.` · `ANG 788: ONE LIGHT IN TWO BODIES.` · `ANG 274: WHERE THE EYES REST.` · then, large: `TWO MARRIAGES, ONE PROMISE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a promise at home. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one promise you've made to someone you live with or love. It might be a big one, a vow. It might be small: I'll call on Sundays, I'll take out the trash, I'll be home by six. Sit with that promise for a moment. Notice how it's going, without scolding yourself. Then choose one small way to keep it today, and let that settle into the breath. The bell holds the time.

Faithfulness in marriage. In the Sikh code, fidelity is part of rehat, and adultery is one of the four things the initiated must never do. Guru Amar Das calls a true couple one light in two bodies. Today's word.
Your line: faithful. Today, keep one promise to someone at home exactly as you said you would, even a small one, and notice whether they notice. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-three.
